questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which tract is the main alternative (indirect) pathway to the corticospinal tract for motor control?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus/rubrospinal tract is the principal alternative motor pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Rubrospinal tract: main indirect pathway from cerebellum via red nucleus to spinal cord.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by
questions.explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the TECTOSPINAL tract. Fibers from the superior colliculus cross in the dorsal tegmentum at the inferior colliculus level to descend and control neck muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation: tectospinal tract crosses at inferior colliculus level.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Tectospinal tract origin is......
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract originates from the contralateral superior colliculus and descends to the cervical spinal cord, mediating reflex adjustments of head and neck position in response to visual stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract originates from superior colliculus for head-neck reflexes to visual inputs.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Internal arcuate fibers:
options: Arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Terminate at gracile and cuneate nuclei.
Carry proprioceptive impulses from the head.
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers arise from the gracile and cuneate nuclei, decussate (cross the midline) in the medulla, and ascend as the medial lemniscus to the thalamus. They are the second-order neurons of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers arise from gracile and cuneate nuclei, form medial lemniscus

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: One of the following tracts carries sensations to subcortical level:
questions.explanation: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract carries proprioceptive information to the cerebellum (subcortical level); other tracts listed go to thalamus/cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Spinocerebellar tract function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 45-year-old patient presents with difficulty walking, muscle weakness, and a loss of proprioception (awareness of body position). Imaging reveals a lesion in the spinal cord. Which major ascending tract in the spinal cord is most likely affected, leading to these symptoms?
questions.explanation: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carries proprioception, vibration sense, and fine discriminative touch from the body to the thalamus and then to the somatosensory cortex. Lesions cause loss of proprioception, vibration sense, and stereognosis. The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature; the corticospinal tract carries motor signals; spinocerebellar tracts carry proprioceptive data to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway = proprioception, vibration, fine touch; its lesion causes sensory ataxia and positive Romberg.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with difficulty in walking, a loss of proprioception (awareness of body position), and a positive Romberg sign (swaying or falling when asked to stand with eyes closed). Imaging reveals a lesion in the spinal cord. Which neural tract is most likely affected in this case?
questions.explanation: The dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway carries proprioception, vibration sense, and fine (discriminative) touch. A lesion causing loss of proprioception and a positive Romberg sign (swaying/falling with eyes closed) indicates dorsal column damage. The spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature; the corticospinal tract carries motor signals; spinocerebellar tracts carry proprioceptive information to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Loss of proprioception, vibration sense, stereognosis, and positive Romberg sign = dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway lesion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following tracts DON'T extend to all segment of spinal cord?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract is present only in upper cervical segments (C1-C6/8), originating from the tectum of midbrain. It does not extend to all spinal cord levels, unlike the vestibulospinal and reticulospinal tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract does NOT extend to all spinal segments (present only in upper cervical)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The ventral tegmental decussation is formed by
questions.explanation: The VENTRAL tegmental decussation is formed by the RUBROSPINAL tract. Fibers from the red nucleus cross in the midbrain (at superior colliculus level) to descend and control limb flexor muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral tegmental decussation: rubrospinal tract crosses at superior colliculus level.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The superior colliculus of midbrain is formed of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The superior colliculus has layers: stratum zonale (superficial), stratum opticum, stratum lemnisci, and stratum basale (deep). The dorsal tegmental tract is a fiber tract, not part of the colliculus structure.
questions.keyConcept: Superior colliculus layers: zonale, opticum, lemnisci, basale (NOT dorsal tegmental tract)

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Dorsal tegmental decussation:
options: Its fibers descend in all segments of spinal cord.
Present in inferior level of midbrain.
questions.explanation: The dorsal tegmental decussation is formed by the TECTOSPINAL tract, which crosses at the level of the inferior colliculus in the midbrain. It descends to control neck muscles in response to visual stimuli. It is not the rubrospinal tract and does not descend in all spinal segments.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal tegmental decussation: tectospinal tract crosses at inferior colliculus level, controls neck muscles.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which extrapyramidal tract helps adjust the head and neck in response to visual and cutaneous stimuli?
questions.explanation: The tectospinal tract originates from the superior colliculus and carries reflexes related to head and neck movement in response to visual stimuli, decussating at the midbrain.
questions.keyConcept: Tectospinal tract mediates reflex head movements toward visual stimuli, crossing at midbrain level.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Proprioceptive sensation from the big toe ascends to the brainstem through which fibers?
questions.explanation: Proprioception from the lower limb ascends via the gracile fasciculus in the posterior columns to the gracile nucleus in the medulla, then decussates as internal arcuate fibers to form the medial lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile fasciculus carries lower limb proprioception to the medulla before decussation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: In a patient with an upper motor neuron lesion, superficial reflexes (e.g., abdominal reflex) are absent. Which tract is most likely intact?
questions.explanation: Upper motor neuron lesions abolish superficial reflexes (abdominal, cremasteric) due to disruption of descending cortical facilitation to spinal interneurons.
questions.keyConcept: UMN lesions eliminate superficial reflexes by removing cortical facilitation to spinal reflex arcs.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which tract is responsible for spino‑visual reflexes (turning the head and eyes toward a cutaneous stimulus)?
questions.explanation: The spinotectal tract carries pain information to the superior colliculus for reflex head and eye movements toward cutaneous stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Spinotectal reflex

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sacral fibers are the most medial fibers in the spinal cord during its ascend through:
questions.explanation: In the gracile tract, sacral fibers are located most medially (near the posterior median sulcus) while cervical fibers are most lateral. This somatotopic arrangement is maintained throughout the tract.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers most medial in gracile tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Unconscious proprioception from the biceps brachii is carried primarily by which tract?
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract carries proprioception from the upper limb (including biceps brachii) and synapses in the cuneate nucleus of the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Upper limb proprioception tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding Crude Touch sensation:
options: Is perceived at the level of the sensory cortex
Is transmitted through dorsal column pathway
Is better felt in non-hairy skin areas
It is one of the protopathic sensations
questions.explanation: Crude touch is one of the protopathic (primitive) sensations along with pain and temperature. It is transmitted through the anterior spinothalamic tract (not dorsal column), perceived at the level of the thalamus (not cortex), and uses free nerve endings (not Meissner's corpuscles).
questions.keyConcept: Protopathic sensations (crude touch, pain, temperature) travel via anterolateral system; epicritic (fine touch, vibration) via dorsal column.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Unconscious proprioception from the upper limb (elbow/wrist) is carried by the:
questions.explanation: The cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneocerebellar tract carries unconscious proprioception from upper limb to cerebellum.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Hemisection of the spinal cord most likely produces which finding?
options: Loss of all types of sensation of the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Loss of proprioception of the opposite side below the level of the lesion
Loss of dorsal column sensations of the same side below the level of the lesion
Lower motor neuron lesion of the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Upper motor neuron lesion of the opposite side at the level of the lesion
questions.explanation: Spinal cord hemisection produces the classic Brown-Sequard pattern: ipsilateral upper motor neuron paralysis, loss of proprioception and vibration sense, with contralateral loss of pain and temperature beginning a few segments below.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection causes classic Brown-Sequard syndrome with dissociated sensory loss and UMN signs.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All statements about ventral spinothalamic tract are true Except:
options: Is concerned with crude touch and pressure.
Its fibers decussate in the medulla oblongata.
Terminates in ventral posterolateral nucleus of thalamus.
Shares in formation of spinal lemniscus.
Lies in the anterior white column.
questions.explanation: The ventral spinothalamic tract decussates at the spinal cord level (not medulla) before ascending. It carries crude touch and pressure, lies in the anterior white column, and terminates in VPL of thalamus.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral spinothalamic decussates at spinal cord level

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following inhibits pain sensation?
options: Activation of the lateral spinothalamic tract
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation activates descending pain inhibition pathways, reducing pain transmission at the spinal cord level.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid pain inhibition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The spinal tract involved with the control of trunk muscles is:
questions.explanation: The anterior corticospinal tract descends from the motor cortex in the lateral column but then crosses in the spinal cord (anterior white commissure) and supplies the TRUNK muscles (axial and proximal limb muscles). It is involved in fine control of trunk posture and proximal limb movements. The lateral corticospinal tract controls limb muscles.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior corticospinal tract controls axial/trunk muscles; decussates in spinal cord. Lateral corticospinal tract controls limb muscles.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which tract continues as the neospinothalamic pathway carrying pain and temperature sensations to the thalamus?
questions.explanation: The neospinothalamic tract carries fast, sharp pain and temperature via lateral spinothalamic fibers. It ascends through the brainstem and terminates in the ventral posterolateral (VPL) thalamic nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Neospinothalamic tract conveys rapid, well-localized pain via direct pathway to thalamus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 32-year-old male patient presents with a loss of lower extremity motor control on the left side. He exhibits a Babinski sign and has increased deep tendon reflexes in the left lower extremity. He has no loss of sensation. The structure lesioned in the spinal cord is the:
questions.explanation: Left lower limb motor weakness with Babinski sign and increased deep tendon reflexes (UMN signs) indicates a lesion of the LEFT lateral corticospinal tract. The corticospinal tract decussates in the medulla (pyramidal decussation), so a lesion below this level affects the IPSILATERAL side below the lesion. Left corticospinal tract lesion causes left-sided weakness.
questions.keyConcept: Left corticospinal tract lesion = LEFT lower limb weakness with UMN signs (Babinski, hyperreflexia); tract decussates in medulla.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Conscious proprioception from right lower limb are carried by:
options: Tracts of left posterior white column.
questions.explanation: Conscious proprioception from the right lower limb is carried by the right gracile tract, which ascends ipsilaterally in the posterior column and decussates in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract is ipsilateral for lower limb proprioception

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The ability to recognize an unseen familiar object placed in the hand depends on the integrity of which tract?
questions.explanation: Recognizing a familiar object by touch (stereognosis) requires fine touch and proprioception, carried by the cuneate tract from the upper limb. The gracile tract carries these sensations from the lower body.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract carries fine touch from upper limb

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Tegmentum pontis contains all the following structures EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: The parasympathetic nucleus of the glossopharyngeal nerve is the inferior salivary nucleus. It provides parasympathetic innervation to the parotid gland via the otic ganglion.
questions.keyConcept: Inferior salivary nucleus - parasympathetic to parotid

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which thalamic nuclei receive input from the paleospinothalamic tract?
questions.explanation: The paleospinothalamic tract (archispinothalamic) carries slow, dull pain and temperature to the intralaminar nuclei of the thalamus, which project diffusely to association cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Paleospinothalamic tract terminates in intralaminar thalamic nuclei for poorly localized pain.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Ventral spinothalamic tract is:
questions.explanation: The ventral spinothalamic tract crosses at the spinal cord level and ascends through the brainstem, eventually reaching the thalamus via the spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral spinothalamic tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient with a spinal cord lesion has loss of vibration and position sense in both legs but normal pain and temperature sensation. Which tract is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Bilateral loss of vibration and position sense with preserved pain/temperature indicates gracile tract lesion, as it carries proprioception and vibration from the legs.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile tract lesion

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Unconscious proprioception is carried by:
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception, which does not reach conscious awareness, is carried to the cerebellum by the anterior and posterior spinocerebellar tracts.
questions.keyConcept: Spinocerebellar tracts carry unconscious proprioception

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The right spinal lemniscus carries sensations of:
options: Pain and temperature from left side of the body.
Conscious proprioception from left side of the body.
Muscle tone from right side of body.
questions.explanation: The spinal lemniscus is formed by fibers of the spinothalamic tracts after they decussate. Pain and temperature from the left body crosses to the right spinal lemniscus.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus carries contralateral pain/temperature

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The cuneate tract carries which of the following sensations?
options: Crude touch from upper & lower limbs.
Fine touch from upper & lower limbs.
Unconscious proprioception from upper and lower limbs.
questions.explanation: The cuneate tract carries fine (discriminative) touch from the upper limb only. Crude touch from upper limb is carried by the ventral spinothalamic tract. Lower limb fine touch uses the gracile tract.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract carries fine touch from upper limb only

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 28-year-old patient is involved in a car accident and sustains a traumatic injury to their spinal cord. As a result, they lose motor function below the waist and have no sensation in their lower limbs. Based on the location of the injury, which region of the spinal cord is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: Loss of motor function below the waist and no sensation in lower limbs indicates a lesion affecting the lumbar and sacral regions of the spinal cord. The lumbar spinal cord segments (L1-L5) are located around T11-L1 vertebral levels. The cervical region controls the upper limbs; thoracic region controls the trunk. In this adult, the lesion is in the lower spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Motor and sensory loss in lower limbs = lumbar/sacral spinal cord region; controls lower limb movement and sensation.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 50-year-old female patient presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of right-sided hemiparesis. She reports that she woke up this morning and was unable to move her right arm or leg. Which of the following anatomical areas of the brain is most likely affected in this patient?
options: The opercular and triangular parts of the inferior frontal gyrus
Superior lip of posterior ramus of lateral sulcus
questions.explanation: The precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex) in the frontal lobe is the region responsible for voluntary motor control. Hemiparesis (weakness of right arm and leg) indicates a lesion in the LEFT precentral gyrus (contralateral to the affected side). The postcentral gyrus is somatosensory; the angular gyrus is for reading and language; Broca's area is for speech production.
questions.keyConcept: Right-sided hemiparesis = lesion in the LEFT precentral gyrus (primary motor cortex); contralateral motor control.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Syringomyelia first affects
options: Pain and temperature on both sides of the body
Pain and temperature on one side of the body
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia (fluid-filled cavity in central spinal cord) first affects crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia sensory loss pattern

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Loss of pain and temperature sensation from the face, with involvement of the corresponding ascending pathway, indicates a lesion in which of the following?
questions.explanation: Loss of pain/temperature on the same side of face (trigeminal) with opposite body side indicates a lesion at the junction of medulla and spinal cord affecting the spinal trigeminal nucleus and lateral spinothalamic tract.
questions.keyConcept: Alternating sensory loss (ipsilateral face, contralateral body) localizes to the craniocervical junction.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Loss of sensation from the left upper limb indicates a lesion in which of the following areas?
questions.explanation: The left upper limb sensory representation is in the right postcentral gyrus (postcentral gyrus), located in the parietal lobe, specifically the upper part near the central sulcus.
questions.keyConcept: Upper limb somatosensory cortex is located in the postcentral gyrus, above the lateral sulcus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Posterior column lies between:
questions.explanation: The posterior (dorsal) column lies between the posterior median septum and the posterior horn, carrying proprioception and fine touch sensation.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior column location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Anterior column lies between:
questions.explanation: The anterior column lies between the anterior median fissure and the anterior horn, containing motor neurons for voluntary movement.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior column location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lateral column lies between:
questions.explanation: The lateral column lies between the anterior and posterior columns, containing ascending sensory and descending motor pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral column location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Spinal lemniscus made by joining:
questions.explanation: The spinal lemniscus is formed by the union of ventral and lateral spinothalamic tracts, carrying pain and temperature sensation through the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus composition

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following can be found in a patient diagnosed with syringomyelia?
options: loss of pain and temperature in the upper limbs and chest.
loss of touch in the upper limbs and chest
loss of pain and temperature in the abdomen and lower limbs
loss of touch in the abdomen and lower limbs
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia damages crossing spinothalamic fibers causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature in a cape-like distribution over upper limbs and chest.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia presentation

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A female patient has reduced pain and temperature sense in upper limbs and chest but her sense of tactile discrimination is perfectly normal in these areas. State which tract/tracts is/are involved and name the disease.
options: Lateral spinothalamic and gracile – Tabes dorsalis.
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia damages the crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature with preserved tactile discrimination.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia mechanism

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which receptor is specialised for tactile discrimination and two‑point discrimination?
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles in the dermal papillae detect fine touch, texture, and two-point discrimination; they adapt rapidly and are numerous in fingertips.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner corpuscle function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Clark’s nucleus (dorsal nucleus) is located in which lamina?
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is located in Rexed lamina VII at T1-L2 levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus lamina

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Contralateral sensation from the face and body is represented in the:
questions.explanation: SI (areas 3,1,2) maps the contralateral half of the body and face.
questions.keyConcept: Face represented upside down in somatosensory cortex, with larger areas for lips and fingers.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The lateral most fibers of the spinothalamic tract:
questions.explanation: The spinothalamic tracts show somatotopic organization where sacral fibers are most lateral (superficial) and cervical fibers are most medial (deep). This arrangement is preserved as fibers ascend through the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers are most lateral in spinothalamic tract

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from which nucleus?
questions.explanation: The dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from Clarke's nucleus (nucleus dorsalis) located in the intermediate grey matter at T1-L2 levels, carrying proprioceptive information to the cerebellum.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal spinocerebellar tract originates from Clarke's nucleus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Crude touch is carried on which tract?
questions.explanation: Crude touch and pressure are carried by the ventral (anterior) spinothalamic tract. Pain and temperature are carried by the lateral spinothalamic tract, while fine touch uses the dorsal columns.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral spinothalamic carries crude touch

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The right medial lemniscus carries sensations of:
options: Pain from the left side of the body.
Conscious proprioception from the left side of the body.
Muscle tone from right side of the body.
Crude touch from the left side of the body.
Fine touch from right side of body.
questions.explanation: The medial lemniscus is formed by second order neurons of the dorsal column pathway (gracile and cuneate). It carries conscious proprioception and fine touch from the contralateral side of the body.
questions.keyConcept: Medial lemniscus carries contralateral fine touch/proprioception

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The postcentral gyrus receives all the following sensations Except:
questions.explanation: The postcentral gyrus is the primary somatosensory cortex. It receives pain and temperature via the spinothalamic pathway, but does not receive muscle tone, which is a motor function.
questions.keyConcept: Postcentral gyrus processes sensory modalities except motor tone

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Sense of movement and sense of position are lost after lesion of:
questions.explanation: Sense of movement (kinesthesia) and position sense are carried by the dorsal column tracts (gracile and cuneate). Loss of these sensations indicates damage to the posterior columns.
questions.keyConcept: Gracile and cuneate tracts carry position/movement sense

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which one of the following sensations has most of its fibers NOT synapsing in the spinal cord?
options: Sensation of pain of left lower limb.
Sensation of crude touch of right upper limb.
Sensation of position of left upper limb.
Sensation of temperature of left big toe.
Sensation of pain of left shoulder.
questions.explanation: Fine touch and conscious proprioception from the upper limb (position sense) do not synapse in the spinal cord; their first order neurons pass directly to the dorsal column nuclei in the medulla.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column sensations bypass spinal synapse

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Syringomyelia first affects:
options: Pain and temperature on both sides of the body.
Pain and temperature on one side of the body.
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia first affects crossing spinothalamic fibers in the central cord, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature while preserving dorsal column functions (touch, proprioception).
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia affects crossing pain/temperature fibers

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient who has a right hemisection of spinal cord at the level of T6 will suffer from all the following EXCEPT:
options: Paralysis of muscles of 6th right intercostal space.
Loss of proprioception of right lower limb.
Loss of fine touch in right upper limb.
Loss of pain & temperature in left lower limb.
questions.explanation: Right hemisection at T6 causes ipsilateral paralysis and proprioception loss in the right lower limb, contralateral pain/temperature loss in the left lower limb. Fine touch from upper limb uses dorsal columns which are unaffected.
questions.keyConcept: Hemisection spares ipsilateral upper limb fine touch

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Persistent pain in big toe is received in:
options: Lower part of post central gyrus.
Upper part of post central gyrus.
questions.explanation: The big toe is represented in the most medial and inferior part of the postcentral gyrus, which continues onto the paracentral lobule. The representation follows a somatotopic pattern with the foot at the medial surface.
questions.keyConcept: Big toe represented at medial postcentral gyrus/paracentral lobule

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The layer rich in neuroblasts in the developing spinal cord is:
questions.explanation: The mantle layer (intermediate zone) of the developing spinal cord is rich in NEUROBLASTS (developing neurons) and is located between the ventricular zone (ependymal layer) and the marginal zone. The alar plate neuroblasts form the dorsal horn (sensory); the basal plate neuroblasts form the ventral horn (motor).
questions.keyConcept: Mantle layer (intermediate zone) contains neuroblasts; alar plate forms dorsal horn; basal plate forms ventral horn.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following might be the location of lesion in this patient? (referring to Question 31)
questions.explanation: In Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection of spinal cord), the lesion affects the ipsilateral corticospinal tract (motor paralysis) and ipsilateral dorsal column (loss of proprioception/vibration) below the lesion, while the contralateral spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature) is lost because it crosses within one or two segments. Left motor deficit + right pinprick loss = LEFT cord hemisection. At C8 level, this causes motor weakness in the left lower limb and sensory loss on the right below C8.
questions.keyConcept: Left motor + right pain loss = LEFT Brown-Sequard syndrome. Left C8 cord hemisection causes left lower limb weakness and right C8-dermatome pain loss.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient with a traumatic lesion of the left half of the spinal cord at the level of the eighth cervical segment might present the following sign(s) and symptom(s):
options: Loss of pain and temperature sensations on the left side below the level of the lesion
Loss of position sense of the right leg
Right-sided lower motor paralysis in the segment of the lesion and muscular atrophy
questions.explanation: In left hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome), the corticospinal tract is damaged on the left side, causing ipsilateral UMN signs below the lesion. Option D is correct because the left corticospinal damage produces left-sided positive Babinski sign below C8. Option A is wrong (pain/temp loss is contralateral in spinothalamic tract damage). Option B is wrong (position sense loss is ipsilateral in dorsal column damage). Option C is wrong (hemiplegia would be ipsilateral, not right). Option E is wrong (LMN signs occur at the lesion level, not below).
questions.keyConcept: In spinal cord hemisection, ipsilateral UMN paralysis and Babinski sign occur below the lesion due to corticospinal tract damage.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Hemisection of spinal cord gives the following symptoms on the same side below the level of lesion:
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome (hemisection of spinal cord): ipsilateral motor weakness and proprioception loss (corticospinal and dorsal columns) BELOW lesion; contralateral pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic) 1-2 segments below lesion.选项D正确. The answer is D. This is the classic dissociated sensory loss pattern.
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral motor/ proprioception loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss - below lesion level.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The ventral grey column of the spinal cord contains the following groups of nerve cells Except
questions.explanation: The ventral grey column contains dorsomedial, ventrolateral, intermediolateral, and central groups; the retrodorsolateral group is found in the dorsal horn (lamina IX), not ventral horn.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral horn neuronal groups

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The gracile and cuneate tracts of the spinal cord are supplied by
questions.explanation: The gracile and cuneate tracts are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries (branches of vertebral artery) and radicular arteries; the anterior spinal artery supplies anterior cord structures.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column arterial supply

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Hemisection of spinal cord gives the following symptoms on the same side below the level of lesion
questions.explanation: In spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard), ipsilateral loss below lesion includes proprioception (dorsal columns) and upper motor neuron signs (corticospinal tract); pain/temperature loss is contralateral (spinothalamic decussation).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard ipsilateral signs

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The following occur in Brown Sequard Syndrome Except
options: Ipsilateral UMN lesion below level of lesion
Contralateral loss of exteroceptive sensations below level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of proprioceptive sensations below level of lesion
Contralateral L.M.N. lesion at same level of lesion
Ipsilateral loss of pain and temperature at same level of lesion
questions.explanation: In Brown-Sequard syndrome, the LMN lesion at the level of lesion is ipsilateral (not contralateral); the lesion involves corticospinal tract (ipsi UMN signs) and dorsal columns (ipsi proprioception).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard LMN lesion side

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following correctly pairs a neural structure with its functional role?
options: Spinothalamic tract – conscious proprioception from lower limb
Cuneate nucleus – unconscious proprioception from upper limb
Gracile nucleus – conscious proprioception from lower limb
Dorsal spinocerebellar tract – unconscious proprioception from upper limb
Ventral spinocerebellar tract – unconscious proprioception from upper limb
questions.explanation: The dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway carries fine touch, vibration, and proprioception. The nucleus cuneatus (not gracilis) receives upper limb proprioception. Gracilis nucleus receives lower limb input.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column pathways are modality-specific: cuneatus for upper limb, gracilis for lower limb.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which tracts carry kinesthetic sensation from the body?
questions.explanation: Kinesthetic sensation (joint position, movement) travels via the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway: gracile fasciculus for lower body, cuneate fasciculus for upper body.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal columns are the exclusive pathway for conscious proprioception and kinesthesia.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Unconscious proprioception from the wrist is carried through which of the following tracts?
questions.explanation: Unconscious proprioception from the upper limb is carried by cuneospinocerebellar fibers that travel in the inferior cerebellar peduncle to the cerebellum (not the dorsal columns which carry conscious proprioception).
questions.keyConcept: Cuneospinocerebellar tract carries unconscious upper limb proprioception via inferior cerebellar peduncle.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient presents with sudden onset bilateral paraplegia and loss of pain and temperature sensation below a certain level. The most likely cause is:
questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery syndrome causes bilateral motor paralysis (corticospinal tracts) and loss of pain/temperature (spinothalamic tracts) below the lesion, with preserved proprioception (dorsal columns supplied by posterior spinal arteries).
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery occlusion causes bilateral motor and pain/temperature loss with preserved proprioception.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: 30-year-old male suffers a traumatic injury to his spine. He cannot move his legs and has lost all sensation below the level of the injury. Most likely diagnosis:
options: Complete spinal cord transection at C4
Complete spinal cord transection at T5
Complete spinal cord transection at T8
Hemisection of spinal cord at T12
questions.explanation: Bilateral leg weakness and loss of pain/temperature suggest anterior cord syndrome from anterior spinal artery occlusion. Posterior column function (proprioception) is preserved because they are supplied by posterior spinal arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior cord syndrome spares dorsal columns while affecting lateral corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Right hemisection of the spinal cord most likely produces which finding?
options: Loss of all types of sensation of the left side at the level of the lesion
Loss of proprioception of the left side below the level of the lesion
Loss of pain and temperature sensations of the left side below the level of the lesion
Left lower motor neuron lesion at the level of the lesion
Left upper motor neuron lesion at the level of the lesion
questions.explanation: Right spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome) causes ipsilateral motor paralysis and proprioception loss below the lesion, with contralateral pain/temperature loss starting 1-2 segments below.
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard syndrome: ipsilateral UMN paralysis and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Loss of proprioception on the same side of a lesion with loss of pain and temperature on the opposite side is characteristic of which condition?
options: Complete spinal cord transection at C4
Complete spinal cord transection at T5
Complete spinal cord transection at T8
Complete spinal cord transection at T12
questions.explanation: This pattern describes Brown-Sequard syndrome where ipsilateral proprioception (dorsal column) is lost with contralateral pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic) due to hemisection of the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral proprioception + contralateral pain loss indicates hemisection (Brown-Sequard syndrome).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: ........... tactile localization, discrimination
questions.explanation: Fine (discriminative) touch enables tactile localization and two-point discrimination, mediated by Meissner corpuscles and Merkel discs traveling via the dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Fine touch function

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All receptors of fine touch except:
questions.explanation: Fine touch receptors include Meissner corpuscles, Merkel discs, and Ruffini endings; tendon spindles are proprioceptive receptors, not tactile.
questions.keyConcept: Fine touch receptors

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Receptors of crude touch are:
questions.explanation: Crude (light) touch receptors include Meissner corpuscles, Merkel discs combined with free nerve endings, and peritrichial (hair follicle) nerve endings.
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch receptors

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Receptors of pain, temperature are:
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are the receptors for pain and temperature sensation throughout the body; they are the most primitive and widely distributed sensory receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Pain temperature receptors

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All characters of pain, temperature pathway except:
options: enter lateral division of posterior root
medium cell in spinal ganglia that enter medial division of posterior root
questions.explanation: Pain and temperature pathway uses small cells in dorsal root ganglia entering via the lateral division (not medium cells entering medially).
questions.keyConcept: Pain pathway characteristics

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: If a patient cannot recognize an unseen familiar object placed in his hand, the sensory tract that might be affected is:
questions.explanation: Stereognosis (recognition of objects by touch) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway; cuneate tract carries this from the upper limb.
questions.keyConcept: Stereognosis pathway

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The plexus of Bonnet is best described as:
options: A capsulated receptor with concentric lamellae
questions.explanation: The plexus of Bonnet (hair follicle receptor network) is a mechanoreceptor formed by free nerve endings that wrap around hair follicles to detect hair movement.
questions.keyConcept: Plexus of Bonnet

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which receptors are located most deeply in the skin (dermis and hypodermis)?
options: Krause end bulb and free nerve endings
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles and Ruffini endings are the deepest tactile receptors, located in the dermis and hypodermis for vibration and stretch detection.
questions.keyConcept: Deep skin receptors

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient with syringomyelia typically loses pain and temperature sensation in the upper limbs but retains touch and vibration. Which tract is damaged?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia damages the crossing fibers of the lateral spinothalamic tract in the cervical region, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature while preserving dorsal column functions like touch and vibration.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia: lateral spinothalamic tract damaged, losing pain/temperature but preserving touch/vibration.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient has loss of pain and temperature on the right side of the body and loss of proprioception on the left side below the level of a spinal cord lesion. This pattern is characteristic of:
questions.explanation: This pattern describes Brown-Sequard syndrome: ipsilateral motor and proprioceptive loss (corticospinal and dorsal columns) below the lesion with contralateral pain/temperature loss (lateral spinothalamic crossing fibers).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard: ipsilateral motor and proprioception loss, contralateral pain loss below lesion.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Choose the correct statement about the sensory homunculus:
options: It is the body representation within the motor cortex.
Somatosensory cortex corresponds point by point with regions in ipsilateral side of the body.
The body is represented upside down.
The body representation depends on the size of the target part.
questions.explanation: The sensory homunculus represents the body upside-down (inverted) in the postcentral gyrus, with larger representations for areas with higher receptor density like lips and fingertips.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory homunculus: body represented upside-down in postcentral gyrus.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Regarding the development of the spinal cord, choose the incorrect combination:
options: The lumen of the neural tube – the central canal.
The alar lamina – the ventral horns of the grey matter.
Neurons opposite the sulcus limitans – lateral horns of the grey matter.
The marginal layer – the white matter.
questions.explanation: The alar lamina (sensory) forms the dorsal horns of grey matter, while the basal lamina (motor) forms the ventral horns - the statement incorrectly matches them.
questions.keyConcept: Alar lamina: dorsal horns; Basal lamina: ventral horns.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The right spinal lemniscus carries sensations of
options: Pain and temperature from left side of the body
Conscious proprioception from left side of the body
Muscle tone from right side of body
questions.explanation: The right spinal lemniscus carries pain and temperature sensation from the left side of the body (crossed fibers from spinothalamic tract); proprioception is carried in the dorsal column-medial lemniscus pathway.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal lemniscus crossed pain/temperature

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The lateral most fibers of the dorsal column tract:
questions.explanation: The dorsal column tracts (gracile and cuneate) carry conscious proprioception and fine touch. The lateralmost fibers in the dorsal column represent sacral segments, which ascend most medially in the spinal cord.
questions.keyConcept: Sacral fibers are most lateral in dorsal columns

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lateral spinothalamic tract carries the sensations of:
questions.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensations. The ventral spinothalamic carries crude touch, while the dorsal columns carry fine touch, vibration, and proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral spinothalamic carries pain and temperature

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A patient has a lesion affecting the dorsal column tracts. Which artery is most likely affected?
questions.explanation: The dorsal columns (gracile and cuneate fasciculi) are supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, which are branches of the vertebral arteries.
questions.keyConcept: Posterior spinal arteries supply the dorsal columns, unlike the anterior spinal artery supplying the cord anteriorly.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A branch from cavernous part of internal carotid artery is:
questions.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain from the right lower limb, which was affected. The ipsilateral loss of vibration sense indicates dorsal column involvement (gracile tract for lower limb). The UMN signs and the pattern of sensory loss indicate a right hemisection (Brown-Sequard) at T6 level.
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard syndrome causes ipsilateral motor and contralateral pain loss

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Lesion of the anterior spinal artery most likely produces which finding?
questions.explanation: Anterior spinal artery syndrome causes bilateral loss of motor function (corticospinal tracts) and pain/temperature sensation (spinothalamic tracts), with dorsal column function (proprioception, vibration) preserved.
questions.keyConcept: Anterior spinal artery supplies corticospinal and spinothalamic tracts; dorsal columns are supplied by posterior arteries.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: All receptors of proprioception except:
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, tendon spindles (Golgi tendon organs), and joint receptors; Merkel discs are tactile receptors, not proprioceptive.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception receptors

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors include muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, and joint receptors (Pacinian corpuscles at joints), providing limb position sense.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioception receptors

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Gamma motor neurons are found in which lamina of the spinal cord?
questions.explanation: Gamma motor neurons are located in Rexed lamina IX of the anterior horn, innervating intrafusal muscle fibers within muscle spindles.
questions.keyConcept: Gamma motor neuron location

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Which of the following is a common microscopic feature between muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ?
options: They are both present in series with extrafusal fibres.
They both respond only to active contraction.
questions.explanation: Both muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs are encapsulated receptors with connective tissue capsules surrounding their sensory endings, distinguishing them from free nerve endings.
questions.keyConcept: Both muscle spindle and Golgi tendon organ are encapsulated receptors.

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: The first order neuron of pain pathway from face is:
questions.explanation: The first order neuron for pain from the face is the pseudounipolar neuron in the trigeminal ganglion. Its peripheral process receives pain from the face, and central process enters the brainstem.
questions.keyConcept: Trigeminal ganglion is 1st neuron for face pain

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: A 20-year-old man presents to the clinic with a chief complaint of burning sensation in his forehead for 3 days duration, that lately is developing vesicles. He reported a history of a sever attack of common cold that resolved a week ago. A herpes Zoster infection was diagnosed. What is the most likely nerve involved in his complaint
questions.explanation: Herpes zoster on the forehead following a common cold (prodromal viral infection) indicates shingles of the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1). The forehead is supplied by the supraorbital and supratrochlear nerves (terminal branches of V1). The frontal nerve is the largest branch of the ophthalmic division. Ramsay Hunt syndrome affects CN VII.
questions.keyConcept: Herpes zoster on forehead = ophthalmic division of trigeminal nerve (CN V1) involvement (shingles).

questions.subject: anatomy
questions.question: Loss of sensation from both the left face and left body indicates a lesion in which of the following areas?
questions.explanation: Loss from both left face and left body indicates a lesion at the left principal sensory nucleus of trigeminal (for face) combined with left medial lemniscus (for body), which is the lateral pontine tegmentum.
questions.keyConcept: ipsilateral face and body sensory loss indicates a lesion affecting both trigeminal and spinothalamic pathways.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: One of the following is NOT a character of Meissner’s corpuscle:
options: It is an encapsulated nerve ending.
It is present in dermal papillae.
The Schwann cells are arranged in two cores.
The nerve fibers run spirally between the Schwann cells.
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscle has Schwann cells arranged in horizontal stacks (not spirally). The nerve fiber runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks. Merkel's disc has nerve fibers running spirally. Meissner's is encapsulated, in dermal papillae, and responds to light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: Schwann cells in horizontal stacks, nerve fibers spiral; light touch receptor in dermal papillae.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Krause end bulb, all true except:
questions.explanation: Krause end bulbs have spherical structures with a gelatinous core, function as cold receptors, and are found in conjunctiva and oral cavity. They are mechanoreceptors. The statement about flattened Teloglia cells is incorrect - they have a different structure.
questions.keyConcept: Krause end bulb: cold receptor, mechanoreceptor, gelatinous core, found in conjunctiva and mouth.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Pacinian corpuscle:
options: Lies in dermal papillae of skin.
Nerve fibers run in spiral coarse.
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles have concentric layers of Teloglia (not Schwann cells arranged transversely). They are located deep in the dermis (not dermal papillae), are encapsulated (not non-capsulated), and the nerve fiber runs centrally (not in spiral).
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscle: concentric Teloglia layers, deep dermis, vibration receptor, encapsulated.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The sensory nerve enters the Meissner’s corpuscle from:
questions.explanation: In Meissner's corpuscle, the sensory nerve enters from the SIDE (laterally), not from the lower part or central core. The nerve fiber then runs spirally between the Schwann cell stacks within the corpuscle.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscle: sensory nerve enters from side; nerve fibers spiral between Schwann cell stacks.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: What is the site of Merkel’s tactile disc?
options: Deep layers of the epidermis of the palmer surfaces of hands and planter surfaces of feet
Transitional sites between hairy & non-hairy skin
questions.explanation: Merkel's tactile discs are found in BOTH hairy and non-hairy skin, particularly in the deep layers of epidermis of palms, soles, and at transitional zones between hairy and non-hairy skin. They are slowly adapting touch receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Merkel's disc: deep epidermis of palms/soles and hairy-non hairy skin transitions; slowly adapting touch receptor.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Pacinian corpuscles are found in
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are found in deep tissues including dermis and hypodermis, as well as mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder, and other viscera. They detect deep pressure and vibration. Their wide distribution reflects their role in detecting deep mechanical stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscles: deep dermis, hypodermis, mesenteries, pancreas, urinary bladder - deep pressure/vibration.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Nucleus dorsalis (Claris nucleus), all true except:
options: In the medial aspect of the base of the posterior horn, in level from C8-L3.
Involved in lamina 7 of gray matter.
Give rise to ventral spinocerebellar tract.
questions.explanation: Nucleus dorsalis (Clarke's nucleus) gives rise to the dorsal spinocerebellar tract (not ventral), located in lamina VII at C8-L3 levels. It has large cells with central nucleus, not eccentric nucleus.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus gives rise to DORSAL spinocerebellar tract (not ventral) - FALSE

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which sensation is primarily detected by Meissner’s corpuscles?
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors in the dermal papillae that detect crude touch and tactile discrimination, particularly in glabrous skin.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner corpuscle function

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which statement about Clarke’s nucleus is correct?
options: Clarke’s nucleus is present at all levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all cervical levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all thoracic levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all lumbar levels
Clarke’s nucleus is present at all sacral levels
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus (dorsocentral nucleus) is present at all thoracic levels (T1-L2) and is the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus distribution

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Free nerve endings are widely distributed in
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are the simplest sensory receptors and are widely distributed throughout the body including epidermis, cornea, mucous membranes of visceral organs, and serous membranes. They detect pain, temperature, and crude touch.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings: most widely distributed receptor; detect pain, temperature, crude touch; in epidermis, cornea, viscera.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: What do free nerve endings respond to?
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings respond to noxious (painful), thermal, and crude touch stimuli. They are polymodal receptors capable of detecting multiple stimulus types. Different fiber types (A-delta for pain/temperature, C for pain) mediate these responses.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings: polymodal - respond to painful, thermal, and tactile stimuli via Aδ and C fibers.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Mention the cutaneous encapsulated receptors?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous encapsulated receptors include Meissner's corpuscles (light touch), Pacinian corpuscles (vibration), Ruffini endings (stretch), and Merkel's discs are sometimes considered encapsulated; all have a surrounding connective tissue capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Encapsulated cutaneous receptors

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which correctly describes a feature of Pacinian corpuscles compared to Meissner corpuscles?
options: Pacinian detect light touch, Meissner detect vibration
Pacinian are mainly in non‑hairy skin, Meissner in hairy skin
Pacinian are in epidermis, Meissner in dermis
Pacinian detect temperature, Meissner detect pain
Pacinian have fibers that pass axially through the corpuscle, Meissner fibers are coiled
questions.explanation: In Pacinian corpuscles, the afferent fiber passes axially through the center, while in Meissner corpuscles the nerve fiber has a coiled (tortuous) course between lamellar cells.
questions.keyConcept: Corpuscle structural differences

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which feature characterizes the nerve ending in a Meissner’s corpuscle?
options: Myelinated afferent fiber enters the base of the corpuscle
questions.explanation: The nerve fiber in Meissner's corpuscle has a characteristic tortuous (coiled) course between the lamellar cells, unlike the straight axial course in Pacinian corpuscles.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner corpuscle structure

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which feature is common to both free nerve endings and Merkel’s discs?
options: They are the most numerous sensory receptors in the body
Found in the epidermis of the skin
Arise from subepidermal plexus of nerves
questions.explanation: Both free nerve endings and Merkel's discs are found in the epidermis; free nerve endings detect pain and temperature while Merkel discs detect light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Epidermal receptors

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which sensory receptors penetrate the epidermis?
options: Free nerve endings and Merkel discs
Muscle spindles and Golgi tendon organs
Krause end bulbs and Ruffini endings
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings and Merkel discs both penetrate the epidermis; free nerve endings respond to pain/temperature while Merkel discs mediate light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Epidermal nerve endings

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Regarding the cervical spinal cord, which statement is correct?
options: Substantia gelatinosa receives mostly motor input
Substantia gelatinosa is located in lamina II
Clarke’s nucleus is located in lamina VI
Clarke’s nucleus is found in all cervical segments
Retropostero‑lateral column of cervical segments supplies the distal part of the lower limb
questions.explanation: Substantia gelatinosa (Roland's substance) is located in lamina II of the spinal cord gray matter and processes pain and temperature sensations.
questions.keyConcept: Substantia gelatinosa location

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which structure is found in the cervical segment (internal structures of spinal cord)?
options: Intermediolateral cell column in lamina VII grey matter
Intermediolateral cell column in lamina VII white matter
Clarke’s nucleus in lamina VII grey matter
Clarke’s nucleus in lamina VII white matter
Substantia gelatinosa in lamina VII grey matter
questions.explanation: Clarke's nucleus is found in lamina VII (intermediate gray matter) at cervical levels, serving as the origin of the dorsal spinocerebellar tract.
questions.keyConcept: Clarke's nucleus location

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following tracts lie in the dorsal funiculus?
questions.explanation: The dorsal (posterior) funiculus contains the fasciculus gracilis and fasciculus cuneatus. The rubrospinal tract is in the lateral funiculus; vestibulospinal tract is in the ventral funiculus.
questions.keyConcept: Cuneate tract (fasciculus cuneatus) lies in the dorsal funiculus

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Tactile discrimination (two‑point discrimination) is best tested by:
questions.explanation: Weber's two-point compass test assesses tactile discrimination ability, testing the spatial resolution of Meissner and Merkel receptors.
questions.keyConcept: Two-point discrimination test

questions.subject: histology
questions.question:
Receptor/s for proprioception is/are:
I. Pacinian corpuscle.
II. Meissner’s corpuscle.
III. Ruffini’ corpuscle.
questions.explanation: Ruffini's corpuscles (type II slowly adapting mechanoreceptors) are proprioceptors in joints and skin. Pacinian corpuscles are vibration/pressure receptors, not proprioceptors.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioceptors: muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, Ruffini's (joints). Vibration: Pacinian. Light touch: Meissner's.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following is a receptor for vibration?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting deep pressure and vibration receptors with a characteristic lamellar structure in the dermis.
questions.keyConcept: Vibration receptor

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Destruction of the ventral horn results in one of the following:
questions.explanation: Destruction of the ventral horn (lower motor neuron) causes flaccid paralysis with muscle atrophy, loss of reflexes, and fasciculations. Crude touch (dorsal column), fine touch (dorsal column), and pain sensation (spinothalamic) are not affected.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral horn destruction causes flaccid paralysis (LMN lesion)

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: The distribution of grey and white matter depends on the distribution of:
questions.explanation: Grey matter contains neuron cell bodies and unmyelinated fibers; white matter contains myelinated fibers; the distribution depends on myelin location.
questions.keyConcept: Myelin and matter distribution

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Spinal n. of trigeminal, equivalent to:
questions.explanation: The spinal nucleus of the trigeminal nerve is equivalent to substantia gelatinosa (Rexed lamina II) of the spinal cord dorsal horn. Both are involved in pain and temperature transmission. The main sensory nucleus handles fine touch; Clarke's nucleus is for proprioception.
questions.keyConcept: Spinal nucleus of V = substantia gelatinosa (pain/temp). Main sensory nucleus = epicritic touch.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Crossing fibers of gracile & cuneate tracts are called:
questions.explanation: Internal arcuate fibers are the DECUSSATING (crossing) fibers of the dorsal column-medial lemniscal system. They cross in the sensory decussation of the closed medulla and form the medial lemniscus. External arcuate fibers are cerebellar afferents.
questions.keyConcept: Internal arcuate fibers: cross in sensory decussation → form medial lemniscus. External arcuate: cerebellar afferents.

questions.subject: histology
questions.question: Which of the following tracts are present in the tegmentum pontis?
questions.explanation: The tegmentum pontis (pontine tegmentum) contains all of these: medial longitudinal fasciculus (vestibulo-ocular), spinothalamic tract (pain/temperature), and central tegmental tract (red nucleus to inferior olive).
questions.keyConcept: Pontine tegmentum: MLF, spinothalamic, central tegmental tracts. Basis pontis: corticospinal, transverse pontine fibers.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which opioid antagonist is also used to reduce alcohol craving?
questions.explanation: Naltrexone (opioid antagonist) is used in alcohol dependence treatment by blocking opioid receptors involved in the rewarding effects of alcohol.
questions.keyConcept: Naltrexone alcohol use

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which is a cannabinoid drug used for management of hashish (cannabis) dependence?
questions.explanation: Dronabinol (synthetic THC) is used medically for cannabis dependence, providing agonist effects that reduce withdrawal and craving.
questions.keyConcept: Cannabinoid dependence treatment

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: All the following are involved in the mechanism of action of morphine Except
options: Most effects are mediated by activation of kappa receptors
Inhibition of calcium influx resulting in inhibition of transmitter release
Increase in K outflux resulting in hyperpolarization of neuronal membrane
Reduction of emotional response to pain
questions.explanation: Morphine's effects are primarily mediated by mu (not kappa) opioid receptors; it also inhibits calcium influx (reducing transmitter release), increases K+ efflux (causing hyperpolarization), and reduces emotional pain response.
questions.keyConcept: Mu vs kappa opioid receptor activation

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The pain analgesic system includes which structure?
options: Local cord neurons which secrete serotonin
Local cord neurons which secrete endorphin
questions.explanation: The periaqueductal gray matter in the midbrain is a key component of the descending pain inhibitory system, connecting to nucleus raphe magnus and inhibiting dorsal horn pain transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Periaqueductal gray is the central controller of descending pain inhibition to dorsal horn.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Addition of the following drugs to L dopa produce all the following except
options: Domperidone / decreases l dopa induced nausea & vomiting
Apomorphine / decreases off time of on-off phenomena
Entacapone / Decrease L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action
questions.explanation: Entacapone DECREASES L-dopa bioavailability and duration of action - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Entacapone inhibits COMT, which DECREASES L-dopa metabolism, thereby INCREASING its bioavailability and duration of action. Domperidone decreases nausea (A is correct). Benztropine decreases absorption (B is correct). Apomorphine decreases off time (C is correct).
questions.keyConcept: COMT inhibitors like entacapone prolong L-dopa action by preventing its peripheral breakdown.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Conscious sedation may be induced by
questions.explanation: Fentanyl with Midazolam induces conscious sedation. Option A is correct. This combination (opioid + benzodiazepine) provides analgesia and amnesia for conscious sedation in minor procedures. Droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia (B). Domperidone is antiemetic (C).
questions.keyConcept: Conscious sedation combines fentanyl (analgesia) with midazolam (anxiolysis/amnesia) for procedural sedation.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following is not common between pethidine & Buprenorphine:
options: Respiratory depression is increased by increasing dose
questions.explanation: Both pethidine and buprenorphine are opioids with similar side effects including analgesia, respiratory depression, nausea/vomiting, and constipation. However, buprenorphine has a ceiling effect on respiratory depression - increasing dose beyond a certain point does not proportionally increase respiratory depression. Pethidine does NOT have this ceiling effect - its respiratory depression increases linearly with dose. This makes buprenorphine safer in overdose. Option B is the correct answer because respiratory depression IS NOT increased proportionally with dose in buprenorphine due to its partial agonist activity at mu receptors, unlike pethidine which shows dose-dependent respiratory depression.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine's ceiling effect on respiratory depression distinguishes it from pethidine's linear dose-dependent depression.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Conscious sedation may be induced by:
questions.explanation: Conscious sedation is achieved by combining a benzodiazepine (for anxiolysis, amnesia, sedation) with an opioid (for analgesia). Fentanyl (opioid) + Midazolam (benzodiazepine) is the classic combination. Fentanyl provides analgesia while midazolam provides anxiolysis and sedation. Option B (Midazolam/Droperidol) - droperidol is used for neuroleptanalgesia, not conscious sedation. Option C (Fentanyl/Domperidone) - domperidone is an antiemetic, not a sedative. Option D is incorrect. The combination allows reduced doses of each drug while achieving adequate sedation and analgesia for procedures like dental work.
questions.keyConcept: Conscious sedation uses fentanyl (analgesic) + midazolam (benzodiazepine) for safe procedural sedation.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Constipation associated with the use of morphine may be relieved by
questions.explanation: Morphine-induced constipation is relieved by stool softeners (docusate), stimulant laxatives, and peripherally-acting opioid antagonists (methylnaltrexone) that don't reverse analgesia.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid-induced constipation treatment

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Neuropathic pain may be managed by
questions.explanation: Neuropathic pain management includes tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline), anticonvulsants (carbamazepine, gabapentin), and atypical opioids (tramadol), all acting on different pain pathways.
questions.keyConcept: Neuropathic pain multimodal management

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Concerning sensory receptors, all the followings are true, Except:
questions.explanation: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily (unlike many other excitable tissues); they maintain responsiveness during sustained stimulation, though they may adapt at different rates.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory receptors do not fatigue easily.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: All the following receptors are phasic receptors Except:
questions.explanation: Free nerve endings are tonic (slowly adapting) receptors that continue firing during sustained stimulation, unlike phasic receptors like Pacinian corpuscles, Meissner's corpuscles, hair end organs, and Merkel's discs which adapt rapidly.
questions.keyConcept: Free nerve endings are tonic receptors; others listed are phasic.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: One of the following anesthetic protocols is NOT correctly matched:
questions.explanation: Neuroleptanalgesia uses droperidol plus fentanyl, NOT propofol - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Neuroleptanalgesia = droperidol (neuroleptic) + fentanyl (opioid). Propofol is used for deep sedation/anesthesia. Options A, B, C are correctly matched.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroleptanalgesia combines droperidol with fentanyl for sedation and analgesia; propofol is a separate anesthetic agent.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following possesses a weak analgesic effect?
questions.explanation: Halothane has weak analgesic effect. Option B is correct. Volatile anesthetics vary in analgesia: halothane provides minimal analgesia, while ketamine (C) and nitrous oxide (A) provide significant analgesia. Fentanyl (D) is a potent opioid analgesic.
questions.keyConcept: Halothane lacks significant analgesic properties, distinguishing it from ketamine and nitrous oxide.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: One of the following anesthetics protocols is not correctly matched:
questions.explanation: Neuroleptanalgesia is the combination of a neuroleptic (droperidol) with an opioid (fentanyl), producing a state of calmness and analgesia without complete unconsciousness. Propofol plus fentanyl is actually IV anesthesia/conscious sedation, not neuroleptanalgesia. The correct combinations: A) Ketamine produces dissociative anesthesia - CORRECT; B) Midazolam + Fentanyl produces conscious sedation - CORRECT; C) Propofol produces deep sedation/anesthesia - CORRECT; D) Propofol + Fentanyl = IV anesthesia, NOT neuroleptanalgesia (which requires droperidol). The answer is D because neuroleptanalgesia specifically refers to droperidol + fentanyl combination.
questions.keyConcept: Neuroleptanalgesia specifically refers to droperidol + fentanyl, producing calmness and analgesia.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following possesses a weak analgesic effect:
questions.explanation: Analgesic potency comparison: Fentanyl > Ketamine > Halothane > Nitrous oxide. Nitrous oxide has WEAK analgesic effect. While N2O provides some analgesia (used in labor, dentistry), its potency is low. Ketamine provides moderate analgesia through NMDA antagonism. Halothane provides minimal analgesia. Fentanyl is a potent opioid with strong analgesic effects. N2O's weak analgesic effect means it's often combined with other agents for surgical procedures. The correct answer is A - nitrous oxide possesses weak analgesic effect compared to the other options.
questions.keyConcept: Nitrous oxide has weak analgesic potency compared to opioids (fentanyl) and ketamine.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Name some strong pure agonists opioids.
questions.explanation: Strong pure agonist opioids include: morphine, heroin, fentanyl, methadone, meperidine, hydromorphone, oxymorphone.选项D正确. The answer is D. These have full agonist activity at mu opioid receptors, providing maximum analgesia but also respiratory depression, sedation, and dependence potential.
questions.keyConcept: Morphine, fentanyl, methadone are strong pure mu opioid agonists - maximum analgesia with respiratory depression risk.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: What are the partial agonists opioids?
questions.explanation: Partial agonist opioids include buprenorphine (partial mu agonist) and pentazocine (partial kappa agonist, mixed agonist-antagonist).选项A正确. Buprenorphine is used for opioid dependence (Suboxone) and analgesia. Its ceiling effect on respiratory depression makes it safer. The answer is A. Pentazocine can precipitate withdrawal in opioid-dependent patients.
questions.keyConcept: Buprenorphine is a partial mu agonist with ceiling effect on respiratory depression - used in opioid dependence treatment.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following concerning zolpidem is not true
options: It is a short acting hypnotic causing less hang over than benzodiazepines
More liable to induce rebound insomnia & disturbance in REM sleep than benzodiazepines.
Its use is associated with less tolerance and dependence than benzodiazepines.
questions.explanation: Zolpidem is LESS liable to induce rebound insomnia than benzodiazepines - this is NOT true. Option C is incorrect. Zolpidem actually has more rebound insomnia potential compared to benzodiazepines because of its short half-life and selective BZ1 receptor action. Options A, B, D are true: zolpidem is short-acting with less hangover, acts on BZ1 receptor, and has less tolerance/dependence than BZDs.
questions.keyConcept: Zolpidem has a short half-life and less hangover than benzodiazepines, but can cause rebound insomnia due to its short duration of action.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following drug is not matched with its mechanism of action
options: Diazepam increases frequency of opening of chloride channels
Zolpidem binds with BZD1 subtype → increases GABA activity
Barbiturates increase duration of opening of chloride channels
questions.explanation: Buspirone is a 5HT1A AGONIST, not antagonist - this is WRONG. Option D is incorrect. Buspirone is a selective 5-HT1A partial agonist (not antagonist). Options A, B, C are correct: diazepam increases frequency of chloride channel opening, zolpidem binds BZ1 receptor, barbiturates increase duration of channel opening.
questions.keyConcept: Buspirone's anxiolytic effect comes from 5-HT1A receptor partial agonism, not antagonism.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following statement is Wrong regarding pharmacokinetics of Benzodiazepines
options: Absorption of intramuscular injection except lorazepam is slower than oral
Metabolized in the liver by oxidation followed by glucuronidation except lorazepam
Clinical duration of action of long acting BDZs is shorter than the actual half life as they form active metabolites
questions.explanation: Clinical duration of long-acting BZDs is longer than actual half-life - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Long-acting BZDs form active metabolites that prolong their effect beyond the parent compound's half-life. Options A, B, D are correct: IM absorption is slower (except lorazepam), lorazepam uses glucuronidation not oxidation, lorazepam has no active metabolites.
questions.keyConcept: Long-acting benzodiazepines have prolonged effects due to active metabolites, making actual duration longer than parent half-life.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following about thiopental is WRONG:
options: Has a rapid onset of action due to rapid crossing of BBB.
Ultra short acting due to rapid metabolism.
Enzyme inducer and may precipitate porphyria.
May induce respiratory depression with no available antidote.
questions.explanation: Thiopental is NOT ultra-short acting due to rapid metabolism - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Thiopental is ultra-short acting due to RAPID DISTRIBUTION out of the brain, not rapid metabolism. It undergoes slow hepatic metabolism but rapid redistribution causes short duration. Options A, C, D are correct: rapid onset, enzyme inducer, no antidote.
questions.keyConcept: Thiopental's ultra-short duration is due to rapid redistribution from brain to other tissues, not rapid metabolism.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is wrong regarding ketamine?
options: Short acting IV agent producing dissociative anesthesia
Useful in hypertension as it decrease blood pressure
questions.explanation: Ketamine INCREASES blood pressure, not decreases - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Ketamine stimulates sympathetic nervous system, causing hypertension and tachycardia. Options A, B, D are correct: short-acting IV dissociative anesthetic, profound analgesia, hallucinations on recovery.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine's sympathomimetic effects cause hypertension and tachycardia, not hypotension.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following drug is characterized by ultra‑short duration of action:
questions.explanation: Midazolam has an ultra‑short duration of action due to rapid redistribution from the brain (half‑life ~1–4 hours), making it ideal for procedural sedation.
questions.keyConcept: Midazolam's ultra‑short duration is due to rapid redistribution, not rapid metabolism.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following statement is wrong regarding pharmacokinetics of benzodiazepines:
options: Absorption of intramuscular injection except Lorazepam is slower than oral
Metabolized in the liver by oxidation followed by glucuronidation except Lorazepam
Clinical duration of action of long acting BZDs is shorter than the actual half-life as they form active metabolites
questions.explanation: Long-acting BZDs (diazepam) form active metabolites (desmethyldiazepam) that have long half-lives. This means their clinical duration of action is LONGER than the actual half-life because active metabolites accumulate and contribute to effects. Option C states 'Clinical duration of action of long acting BZDs is shorter than the actual half-life' which is INCORRECT - it's actually LONGER due to active metabolites. This is why long-acting BZDs can accumulate with repeated dosing and why they have prolonged effects even after the parent drug is cleared.
