questions.keyConcept: Long-acting BZDs have CLONGER clinical duration than half-life due to active metabolite accumulation.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The after discharge in a neuronal pool is based mainly upon the:
questions.explanation: After discharge occurs through reverberatory circuits that maintain neuron firing through positive feedback loops, extending the response beyond the initial stimulus duration.
questions.keyConcept: After discharge: reverberatory circuits maintain firing beyond stimulus.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following statement about halogenated anesthetics is wrong
options: Isoflurane may precipitate ischemia in cardiac patients
Halothane is strong analgesic with medium rate of induction
Desflurane suitable for one day surgery
Sevoflurane is preferred as inhalation agent for children
questions.explanation: Halothane is a WEAK analgesic, not strong - this is WRONG. Option B is incorrect. Halothane provides poor analgesia (unlike nitrous oxide). Volatile anesthetics vary: halothane has slow induction, isoflurane may cause coronary steal, desflurane is for short surgery, sevoflurane is preferred for children (pleasant induction).
questions.keyConcept: Halothane provides minimal analgesia and has slow induction with risk of hepatic toxicity.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is wrong regarding local anesthetics?
options: Binding to plasma protein affects duration of action
Addition of vasoconstrictor shorten duration of action
questions.explanation: Vasoconstrictors PROLONG, not shorten duration - this is WRONG. Option C is incorrect. Epinephrine constricts vessels, decreasing absorption, prolonging duration. Options A, B, D are correct: plasma protein binding affects duration, lipid solubility affects potency, pKa affects onset speed.
questions.keyConcept: Vasoconstrictors added to local anesthetics prolong duration by reducing vascular absorption.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Addition of epinephrine to local anesthetic do not
questions.explanation: Epinephrine does NOT increase potency. Option D is correct. Epinephrine causes vasoconstriction, decreasing absorption (A), prolonging duration (B), and decreasing systemic toxicity (C). It does not affect the intrinsic potency of the local anesthetic molecule.
questions.keyConcept: Epinephrine reduces local anesthetic systemic absorption and toxicity but does not alter drug potency.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: The following anesthetic agent is not acting through increase GABA activity:
questions.explanation: Ketamine produces anesthesia through NMDA receptor antagonism, not GABA enhancement. Mechanism: ketamine is a non-competitive NMDA receptor antagonist that blocks glutamate signaling. Halothane, propofol, and isoflurane all enhance GABA-A receptor activity (though via slightly different mechanisms), leading to increased chloride conductance and neuronal inhibition. Ketamine uniquely preserves cardiovascular function and provides good analgesia, but its NMDA mechanism means it doesn't work through GABA. This makes ketamine useful when GABA-enhancing agents are contraindicated.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine is the only anesthetic listed that acts via NMDA antagonism rather than GABA enhancement.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is ester local anesthetic:
questions.explanation: Ester vs Amide local anesthetics: Esters: procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine, cocaine - metabolized by plasma cholinesterase (short duration). Amides: lidocaine, mepivacaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine - metabolized in liver (longer duration, longer half-life). Benzocaine is a classic ester local anesthetic used topically. Lidocaine (A), bupivacaine (B), and ropivacaine (C) are all amide-type local anesthetics. The correct answer is D - benzocaine is the ester anesthetic. Esters are more prone to causing allergic reactions (para-aminobenzoic acid metabolite).
questions.keyConcept: Benzocaine is an ester local anesthetic, distinguishing it from the amide anesthetics lidocaine, bupivacaine, and ropivacaine.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following is not a characteristic feature of amide local anesthetics:
options: Longer duration of action than ester group
High risk of severe hypersensitivity reaction
Duration of action is prolonged in patient with heart failure
questions.explanation: Amide local anesthetics (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine) have: longer duration than esters (A-true), liver metabolism (B-true), and prolonged action in heart failure due to reduced hepatic blood flow (D-true). However, they have LOW risk of hypersensitivity reactions (esters have high risk due to PABA metabolite). Option C is INCORRECT - amides have LOW risk, not HIGH risk of severe hypersensitivity. This is the NOT characteristic feature, so answer is C. Esters cause more allergic reactions due to para-aminobenzoic acid formation.
questions.keyConcept: Amide local anesthetics have LOW hypersensitivity risk compared to esters (which form allergenic PABA).

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: What are the classifications of local anesthetics?
questions.explanation: Local anesthetics classified by: 1) Chemical structure - esters (procaine, tetracaine, benzocaine) and amides (lidocaine, bupivacaine, ropivacaine); 2) Duration of action - short, intermediate, long-acting.选项C正确. The answer is C. Esters are metabolized by plasma cholinesterase; amides are metabolized in liver.
questions.keyConcept: Local anesthetics are classified as esters vs amides (metabolism) and by duration of action (short/intermediate/long).

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Why are vasoconstrictors added to local anesthetics?
options: To prolong the duration of action
To reduce systemic adverse effects and bleeding tendency
questions.explanation: Vasoconstrictors (epinephrine, norepinephrine, felypressin) are added to local anesthetics to: constrict blood vessels, reduce bleeding, decrease systemic absorption, prolong anesthetic duration, and reduce peak plasma levels.选项C正确. The answer is C. Contraindicated in patients with cardiovascular disease, hyperthyroidism, and those on non-selective beta-blockers.
questions.keyConcept: Vasoconstrictors prolong local anesthetic duration and reduce toxicity by decreasing systemic absorption and bleeding.

questions.subject: pharma
questions.question: Which of the following statements concerning anesthetics is correct ?
options: Thiopental is ultra short acting due to rapid metabolism.
Propofol possesses a strong analgesic effect.
Halothane is the least likely inhalation agent to increase intracranial tension.
Dissociative anesthesia is induced by midazolam.
questions.explanation: Ketamine is a dissociative anesthetic that blocks NMDA (N-methyl-D-aspartate) glutamate receptors, producing anesthesia with catatonia and analgesia. Thiopental is short-acting due to redistribution, not metabolism; propofol lacks analgesic effect; halothane increases ICP.
questions.keyConcept: Ketamine as NMDA receptor antagonist producing dissociative anesthesia

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: What is a contusion in traumatic head injury? And what is its types?
options: Direct parenchymal injury to the brain
Coup injury at the point of impact
Contrecoup injury opposite the point of impact
questions.explanation: Contusion is direct parenchymal brain injury with three types: coup injury at the point of impact, contrecoup injury opposite the impact, and intermediate coup. This includes direct neuronal and glial damage, hemorrhage, and edema. Option D 'All of the above' is correct. Contusions occur from deceleration-acceleration forces causing brain to impact skull. The answer is D. Contusions may evolve into contrecoup injuries due to brain movement within the skull.
questions.keyConcept: Contusions are direct brain injuries including coup (impact), contrecoup (rebound), and intermediate injuries.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: What genetic alterations are associated with pilocytic astrocytomas?
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas are associated with genetic alterations including BRAF fusion (KIAA1549-BRAF) and other MAPK pathway activations. These are low-grade tumors with different genetics from diffuse astrocytomas.选项A正确 - BRAF改变与毛细胞型星形细胞瘤相关. The answer is A. BRAF V600E mutation also occurs but less commonly. These alterations drive MAPK pathway signaling.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytomas harbor BRAF alterations (KIAA1549-BRAF fusion) - distinguishing them from diffuse astrocytomas.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Pilocytic astrocytoma shows the following EXCEPT:
options: Activation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway.
questions.explanation: Pilocytic astrocytomas show activation of the MAPK pathway and BRAF alterations (especially BRAF-KIAA1549 fusion). NF1 inactivation is seen in optic pathway gliomas. IDH1/IDH2 mutations are seen in adult diffuse astrocytomas, not pilocytic.
questions.keyConcept: Pilocytic astrocytoma: BRAF activation, MAPK pathway (NOT IDH1/IDH2 mutations)

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Opening of ligand-gated Cl- channels causes:
options: No change in resting membrane potential.
questions.explanation: Ligand-gated chloride channels (as in GABA-A receptors) increase Cl- conductance, causing hyperpolarization that makes the neuron less likely to fire, resulting in postsynaptic inhibition.
questions.keyConcept: Opening of ligand-gated Cl- channels causes inhibition (hyperpolarization).

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The binding of a neurotransmitter to its receptor at an inhibitory synapse can lead to the ______ of ______ channels.
questions.explanation: At inhibitory synapses, neurotransmitter binding opens potassium channels, allowing K+ efflux that hyperpolarizes the neuron and reduces neuronal excitability.
questions.keyConcept: Inhibitory synapse: opening of potassium channels.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that increases the permeability of Postsynaptic neuron to:
questions.explanation: GABA (gamma-aminobutyric acid) is the main inhibitory neurotransmitter in the CNS, acting by increasing chloride ion permeability through GABA-A receptors.
questions.keyConcept: GABA increases Cl- permeability causing inhibition.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The potency of inhaled anaesthetics is quantitatively defined as the:
questions.explanation: MAC (minimum alveolar concentration) defines potency as the alveolar concentration that prevents movement in 50% of patients to a surgical stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Inhalational anesthetic MAC

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: What is the key genetic finding in oligodendrogliomas?
questions.explanation: The key genetic finding in oligodendrogliomas is codeletion of chromosomes 1p and 19q. This occurs through unbalanced translocation t(1;19)(q10;p10). This codeletion is associated with better prognosis and excellent response to PCV chemotherapy (procarbazine, lomustine, vincristine). Option B is CORRECT. EGFR overexpression (A) is seen in glioblastoma. IDH1 mutation (C) is found in many gliomas but not specific. MDM2 amplification (D) is in some glioblastomas. The answer is B.
questions.keyConcept: 1p/19q codeletion is the hallmark genetic abnormality of oligodendroglioma, predicting better prognosis.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Mention the cutaneous unencapsulated receptors?
questions.explanation: Cutaneous unencapsulated receptors include free nerve endings (pain, temperature), peritrichial endings around hair follicles (light touch), and Merkel's discs (fine touch); all lack a connective tissue capsule.
questions.keyConcept: Unencapsulated cutaneous receptors

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Choose the CORRECT matching:
options: Ganglion – a group of cell bodies within CNS.
Pathway – a chain of successive tracts having different functions.
Lemniscus – a collection of descending fibers within the brain stem.
Afferent – an output going away from a certain structure.
Tract – a bundle of nerve fibers within CNS.
questions.explanation: A tract is a bundle of nerve fibers within the CNS. A pathway is a chain of successive tracts with the same function. A lemniscus is a collection of ascending fibers in the brain stem. Afferent means input toward a structure. A ganglion is a group of cell bodies outside the CNS.
questions.keyConcept: Tract = CNS fiber bundle; pathway = chain of tracts; lemniscus = ascending brainstem fibers

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which statement best describes sensory adaptation?
options: Diminished sensation despite continuous application of the stimulus
Complete absence of sensation after brief stimulus
Activation of additional receptors over time
Conversion of one type of sensation into another
questions.explanation: Sensory adaptation is the decrease in receptor response during sustained stimulation. Slowly adapting receptors maintain response to prolonged stimuli, while rapidly adapting receptors quickly cease firing.
questions.keyConcept: Sensory adaptation reflects receptor capability to maintain (slow) or reduce (rapid) firing during sustained stimuli.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which ion is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during the upstroke of the action potential. Na+ channels open rapidly causing an influx of Na+, creating the spike. K+ is responsible for repolarization during the downstroke.
questions.keyConcept: Sodium ion influx through voltage-gated Na+ channels is responsible for the rapid depolarization phase of the action potential.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which receptor is primarily responsible for maintaining muscle tone?
questions.explanation: Primary endings of muscle spindles (Ia afferents) are primarily responsible for maintaining muscle tone through the stretch reflex arc controlling baseline contraction.
questions.keyConcept: Muscle spindle primary endings provide the major sensory input for tonic stretch reflex and tone maintenance.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT involved in decreasing the activity of the pontine reticular formation?
questions.explanation: The red nucleus is a facilitatory center that INCREASES pontine reticular formation activity, not decreases it. Cortical inhibitory areas, medullary RF, basal ganglia, and corticofugal fibers all decrease pontine RF activity.
questions.keyConcept: Red nucleus facilitates pontine RF; cortical areas, basal ganglia, medullary RF inhibit it.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The phenomenon of decerebrate rigidity can be explained, at least in part, by which of the following?
options: Loss of cerebellar inputs to the red nucleus
Overactivity of the medullary reticular nuclei involved in motor control
Unopposed activity of the pontine reticular nuclei
questions.explanation: Decerebrate rigidity results from loss of pontine reticular nucleus inhibition of medullary reticular nuclei, causing unopposed extensor muscle activity and characteristic rigid posturing.
questions.keyConcept: Decerebrate rigidity: unopposed medullary reticular nuclei activity from pontine loss.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Pain produced by tissue damage is due to release of:
questions.explanation: Tissue damage releases kinins (bradykinin, kallidin) which sensitize nociceptors, causing pain as part of the inflammatory response to injury.
questions.keyConcept: Pain from tissue damage: release of kinins (bradykinin).

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which nitric oxide synthase isozyme is inducible?
questions.explanation: The phagocytic (inducible) nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is calcium-independent and can be induced by cytokines and endotoxin in macrophages during inflammatory responses.
questions.keyConcept: iNOS (phagocytic) is the inducible, calcium-independent NOS isozyme

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The following is not a feature of meningioma:
questions.explanation: Meningiomas typically have a whorled cut surface (not whorly). The other statements about meningioma (adults, benign, psammoma bodies) are true. The question asks for what's NOT a feature.
questions.keyConcept: Meningioma has whorled pattern, not whorly surface - minor terminology

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which type of receptor is found in the cornea?
questions.explanation: The cornea contains abundant free nerve endings (no specific encapsulated receptors) making it extremely sensitive to pain and touch.
questions.keyConcept: Corneal innervation

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: What is the most common position for the appendix?
questions.explanation: The retrocecal position is the most common anatomical position of the appendix, occurring in approximately 65% of individuals. In this position, the appendix lies posterior to the cecum, often tucked behind the ileum. Other less common positions include pelvic (20-30%), subcecal, and preileal. The retrocecal position is clinically significant as it can alter the presentation of appendicitis and may complicate diagnosis.
questions.keyConcept: The retrocecal position is the most common appendix location due to embryological rotation of the cecum.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which receptor helps a blind person read Braille by detecting fine texture and edges?
questions.explanation: Meissner corpuscles detect fine tactile details and edges, enabling blind individuals to read Braille through subtle texture differences.
questions.keyConcept: Braille reading receptors

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following is primarily responsible for rapid depolarization during an action potential?
questions.explanation: Sodium (Na+) is the primary ion responsible for rapid depolarization during the upstroke of the action potential. Na+ channels open rapidly causing an influx of Na+, creating the spike. K+ is responsible for repolarization during the downstroke.
questions.keyConcept: Voltage-gated sodium channels mediate the rapid depolarization phase of action potentials in most neurons and muscle fibers.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following receptors are mechanoreceptors?
questions.explanation: All of these - Merkel's disc, Meissner's corpuscle, and Bounet's plexus (a free nerve ending network) are mechanoreceptors. They transduce mechanical stimuli into neural signals. Merkel's = pressure, Meissner's = light touch, Bounet's = slowly adapting stretch receptor.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanoreceptors: Merkel's (pressure), Meissner's (touch), Bounet's plexus (stretch). All detect mechanical stimuli.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the gate control theory of pain?
options: Pain is transmitted only by large myelinated fibres.
Activity in large afferent fibres can inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
Pain is solely a cortical phenomenon.
Endorphins are released only from the pituitary.
questions.explanation: The gate control theory proposes that large myelinated afferent fibers (touch) can inhibit transmission of pain signals in the dorsal horn through interneurons, effectively 'closing the gate' on pain perception.
questions.keyConcept: Gate control: large afferent fiber activity inhibits dorsal horn pain transmission.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Methyl dopa decreases blood pressure by:
questions.explanation: Alpha-methyl-dopa (methyldopa) decreases blood pressure by acting as a false neurotransmitter: it is converted to methyl-norepinephrine which displaces norepinephrine from sympathetic nerve terminals, reducing sympathetic outflow.
questions.keyConcept: Methyldopa acts as false neurotransmitter displacing norepinephrine to reduce BP

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following nuclei extend in the midbrain:
questions.explanation: The mesencephalic nucleus of the trigeminal nerve extends through the midbrain (alongside the central gray). It is the only sensory nucleus that contains primary afferent cell bodies. Vestibular nuclei are in the pons/medulla. Motor facial is pontine. Superior olive is pontine.
questions.keyConcept: Mesencephalic nucleus of V: only primary afferent neuron in CNS, extends through midbrain.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Crude touch sensation is:
options: Carried in the lateral spinothalamic tract.
Perceived at level of sensory cortex.
questions.explanation: Crude touch is carried by Aδ fibers (lightly myelinated, 2-5 μm diameter, 5-15 m/s conduction). Option A is correct. Option B is wrong (crude touch is poorly localized, fine touch is sharply localized). Option C is wrong (crude touch is carried in anterior spinothalamic tract, not lateral). Option D is wrong (perceived at thalamic level, not cortex). Option E is wrong (receptors for crude touch are phasic, not tonic).
questions.keyConcept: Crude touch uses Aδ fibers and is carried in the anterior spinothalamic tract with poor localization.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Discrimination of stimulus intensity depends mainly on:
questions.explanation: Weber-Fechner law states that discrimination of stimulus intensity depends on the ratio of change to initial stimulus, not absolute difference. Just noticeable difference is proportional to the initial stimulus.
questions.keyConcept: Intensity discrimination depends on proportional Weber fraction rather than absolute stimulus magnitude.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which type of pain is transmitted by Aδ nerve fibers?
questions.explanation: A-delta fibers transmit fast, sharp, well-localized pain (first pain) via the neospinothalamic tract. C fibers transmit slow, dull, poorly localized pain (second pain) via the paleospinothalamic tract.
questions.keyConcept: A-delta fibers mediate fast, localized pain; C fibers mediate slow, diffuse pain.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Fast pain is characterized by which duration?
questions.explanation: Fast pain (A-delta fibers) has a brief duration (~0.1 seconds), occurring immediately after stimulus and enabling rapid localization of noxious stimuli.
questions.keyConcept: Fast pain is brief (~0.1s) and well-localized due to A-delta fiber conduction.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Stereognosis sensation is carried by which neural pathway?
questions.explanation: Stereognosis (recognition of form and texture) requires intact dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway for fine touch and proprioception to reach the sensory cortex.
questions.keyConcept: Dorsal column-medial lemniscal pathway carries stereognosis, fine touch, and proprioception for object recognition.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: In syringomyelia, sensory loss typically follows which pattern?
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes a characteristic 'cape' or 'jacket' distribution sensory loss due to the expansion of the syrinx affecting crossing spinothalamic fibers in the cervical cord.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia cord lesion pattern

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The following sensation is not perceived by Somatosensory A 1:
questions.explanation: Crude touch is transmitted by the anterior spinothalamic tract, not by somatosensory area 1 which processes fine/discriminative touch, vibration, proprioception, and stereognosis.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 does not process crude touch (anterior spinothalamic does).

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Brown-Sequard syndrome is characterized by:
options: Loss of vibration sense on the same side below level of the lesion
Loss of voluntary movements on the opposite side below the level of the lesion
Loss of reflex movements on the opposite side at the level of the lesion
Loss of pain sensation on the same side below the level of the lesion
questions.explanation: Brown-Sequard syndrome: loss of vibration sense on the same side below lesion. Option A is correct. Hemisection causes ipsilateral dorsal column loss (vibration, proprioception) and corticospinal loss (motor) below; contralateral spinothalamic loss (pain, temperature). Options B, C, D are incorrect (motor loss is ipsilateral, reflex loss at lesion level is LMN, pain loss is contralateral).
questions.keyConcept: Brown-Sequard hemisection produces ipsilateral motor and dorsal column loss, contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: 43 year old woman is evaluated in the hospital and is found to have multiple neurologic abnormalities from the level T 12 down. She has loss of vibration and proprioception on the left but these senses are present on the right side. She has absent pain and temperature sensation in the right side from T12 down. Motor power was lost in the left leg but normal motor strength in her right leg. What is the most likely cause of her neurologic symptoms?
options: Complete spinal cord transection at upper thoracic segments.
Complete spinal cord transection at lower thoracic segments.
Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord
Hemisection on the right part of spinal cord
questions.explanation: Hemisection on the left part of spinal cord. Option C is correct. Left hemisection explains: left vibration/proprioception loss (dorsal columns), right pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic), left leg paralysis (corticospinal). Complete transection would affect both sides. Right hemisection would cause opposite findings.
questions.keyConcept: Ipsilateral dorsal column and motor loss with contralateral spinothalamic loss indicates spinal cord hemisection on the side of motor/dorsal column deficits.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Regarding sensory receptors:
options: Receptors are non-specific to stimuli according to Muller’s law
Stimulation of certain receptors can produces different modalities of sensations
Receptors are stimulated by adequate stimuli at a low threshold
Receptor potential is inversely related to the intensity of stimulus according to Weber Fechner law
The same receptor may be stimulated by different stimuli to produce different sensations
questions.explanation: According to Müller's law of specific nerve energies, each receptor is specific to its adequate stimulus. Receptors have LOW threshold for their specific stimulus. Receptor potential is directly proportional to stimulus intensity, not inversely.
questions.keyConcept: Law of specific nerve energies: each receptor responds only to its adequate stimulus at low threshold.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: A reflex arc includes:
options: At least two sets of sequential neurons
At least two sequential sets of central synapses
At least two types of sensory receptors
At least two types of efferent neurons
questions.explanation: A reflex arc requires at minimum a sensory receptor, a sensory neuron, at least one synapse in the CNS, and an efferent motor neuron. This means at least two sets of sequential neurons (afferent and efferent).
questions.keyConcept: Reflex arc components: receptor → afferent neuron → CNS integration → efferent neuron → effector.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following does not contain channels that are activated by mechanical distortion?
questions.explanation: Hair end organs (Ruffini endings) are slowly adapting receptors for skin stretch, not activated by mechanical distortion. Muscle spindles, Pacinian corpuscles, and cochlear hair cells all use mechanically-gated ion channels.
questions.keyConcept: Mechanically-gated channels are found in sensory receptors for touch, pressure, and hearing; Ruffini endings detect static skin stretch rather than vibration.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which type of sensory receptors in the skin respond quickly at the onset of a stimulus but stop firing if the stimulus is constant?
questions.explanation: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors that respond quickly at the onset and offset of a stimulus but cease firing during sustained stimulation due to their large, encapsulated structure.
questions.keyConcept: Pacinian corpuscles are rapidly adapting mechanoreceptors detecting vibration and rapid changes.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which sensory receptor adapts rapidly to sustained skin stimulation?
questions.explanation: Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting receptors in the dermal papillae that adapt quickly to sustained skin stimulation, making them ideal for detecting motion and texture.
questions.keyConcept: Meissner's corpuscles are rapidly adapting tactile receptors in glabrous skin for motion detection.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which stimulates pain receptors?
questions.explanation: Pain receptors (nociceptors) respond to noxious stimuli including intense mechanical distortion, heat (>45C), and chemical irritants (bradykinin, substance P, prostaglandins).
questions.keyConcept: Nociceptors are polymodal free nerve endings responding to mechanical, thermal, and chemical noxious stimuli.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: In secondary hyperalgesia, which describes the affected area?
options: Inflamed tissue directly exposed to noxious stimuli
All dermatomes sharing the same dorsal root ganglion
questions.explanation: Secondary hyperalgesia occurs in the surrounding undamaged tissue adjacent to the primary injury site, where nociceptors become sensitized by inflammatory mediators released from damaged cells.
questions.keyConcept: Secondary hyperalgesia extends beyond the injury site due to central sensitization of dorsal horn neurons.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which explains pain relief when you rub the skin near an injury?
questions.explanation: Rubbing the skin activates A-beta mechanoreceptors that inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn through gating mechanisms in the substantia gelatinosa (gate control theory).
questions.keyConcept: Gate control theory: tactile stimulation inhibits nociceptive transmission via A-beta fiber activation of inhibitory interneurons in dorsal horn.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: A woman wore a dress on the beach. Later, wearing a jacket over the same area caused pain. This is an example of:
options: Increase receptor sensitivity by tissue products
Activity-dependent increase in excitability of dorsal horn neurons
Increased threshold of peripheral nociceptors due to inflammatory mediators
Decreased inhibitory interneuron function in the spinal cord
Impaired saltatory conduction in primary afferent neurons
questions.explanation: Wearing a jacket over tanned skin causes referred pain from sunburned skin, demonstrating referred pain where visceral or deep somatic injury is perceived as cutaneous pain.
questions.keyConcept: Referred pain from deep tissue injury can be perceived as cutaneous pain due to convergence of somatic and visceral afferents on dorsal horn neurons.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which receptors inhibit pain sensation in the CNS?
questions.explanation: Endogenous opioid peptides (endorphins and enkephalins) released from periaqueductal gray and nucleus raphe magnus inhibit pain transmission in the dorsal horn.
questions.keyConcept: Endogenous opioid peptides from brainstem nuclei inhibit nociceptive transmission in the spinal cord dorsal horn.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which statement is true regarding deep pressure sensation?
options: It is mediated by slowly adapting receptors
It is transmitted only by free nerve endings
It adapts rapidly to sustained stimulus
It is carried exclusively by Aδ fibers
It is not associated with vibration
questions.explanation: Deep pressure sensation is transmitted by A-beta fibers via dorsal column pathways and by A-delta fibers via spinothalamic tracts. It has a high threshold compared to light touch.
questions.keyConcept: Deep pressure uses A-beta fibers in dorsal columns and A-delta fibers in spinothalamic tracts.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches a reflex with its sensory receptor?
questions.explanation: The inverse stretch reflex (autogenic inhibition) uses Golgi tendon organs as receptors that inhibit alpha motor neurons when tension becomes dangerous.
questions.keyConcept: Golgi tendon organs mediate inverse stretch reflex to prevent muscle damage from excessive tension.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which accurately describes the pattern of dissociative sensory loss in syringomyelia?
options: Loss of pain and touch with preservation of temperature
Loss of touch and temperature with preservation of pain
Loss of pain with preservation of touch and temperature
Loss of pain and temperature with preservation of touch
Loss of temperature with preservation of touch and pain
questions.explanation: Syringomyelia causes dissociated sensory loss with loss of pain and temperature but preserved touch and proprioception due to damage to crossing spinothalamic fibers in the central canal.
questions.keyConcept: Syringomyelia selectively damages crossing spinothalamic fibers, causing cape-like pain/temperature loss with preserved dorsal column function.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: In Thermal sensations, all of the following are true EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Thermal sensations are carried by Aδ fibers (cold) and C fibers (hot), not Aβ fibers. Aβ fibers carry touch, pressure, and vibration. Cold receptors adapt slower than hot receptors, and maximal discharge occurs at 25°C (cold) and 45°C (hot).
questions.keyConcept: Temperature sensation: Aδ (cold, 10-40°C), C fibers (heat, 30-45°C); transmitted via spinothalamic tract.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Regarding somatosensory area 1 all are correct, Except:
options: Size of representation depends on number of receptors
Have columns that is specialized to receive one type of sensation
questions.explanation: Somatosensory area 1 lies posterior to the central gyrus (postcentral gyrus), not anterior; it receives contralateral input, has columns specialized for single sensation types, and its representation size reflects receptor density.
questions.keyConcept: Somatosensory area 1 lies posterior to central gyrus (postcentral gyrus).

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which is correctly matched regarding the pain analgesic system?
questions.explanation: The periaqueductal gray matter is the origin of descending pain inhibitory pathways that project to nucleus raphe magnus and release opioids to inhibit dorsal horn pain transmission.
questions.keyConcept: PAG is the key origin of descending analgesic pathways utilizing endogenous opioids.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The stretch reflex:
options: Results in relaxation of the stretched muscle.
questions.explanation: Stretch reflex is the fastest body reflex. Option B is correct. It is a monosynaptic reflex with minimal central delay (0.5-0.8 ms). Options A, C, D, E are incorrect: it is monosynaptic (not polysynaptic), receptor is muscle spindle (not Pacinian), has short (not long) central delay, results in contraction (not relaxation).
questions.keyConcept: The monosynaptic stretch reflex has the fastest conduction due to its simple, direct excitatory circuit.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which of the following could NOT be an exteroceptor?
questions.explanation: Muscle spindles are proprioceptors located within muscles that detect stretch and length changes. Exteroceptors receive stimuli from the external environment (thermoreceptors, nociceptors, Pacinian corpuscles, rods/cones).
questions.keyConcept: Proprioceptors like muscle spindles are interoceptors, not exteroceptors which sense external stimuli.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Lesion of the spinocerebellar tract typically produces:
questions.explanation: Spinocerebellar tract lesion causes ipsilateral ataxia and loss of proprioception from the limb, as these tracts carry uncrossed sensory information from muscle spindles and tendon organs.
questions.keyConcept: Spinocerebellar tract damage produces ipsilateral limb ataxia and impaired proprioception.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Which receptors provide the sense of movement and position of the body?
questions.explanation: Proprioception receptors (muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs, joint receptors) provide information about body position, movement, and limb location in space.
questions.keyConcept: Proprioceptive receptors

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: Pain sensation can be inhibited by:
options: Increasing the pain threshold by kinin.
questions.explanation: Opioid receptor stimulation activates descending pain inhibitory pathways from the periaqueductal grey to the dorsal horn, blocking pain signal transmission.
questions.keyConcept: Opioid receptor stimulation inhibits pain sensation.

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: All characters of ventral spinocerebellar tract except:
options: ascend in all level of white matter then brain stem
carry impulse from trunk on same side only
carry impulse from lower limb on same or opposite side
arise from cells in posterior horn (V-VII)
questions.explanation: The ventral spinocerebellar tract carries impulses from the lower limb on both sides (decussates twice) and trunk on the same side, not only trunk on same side.
questions.keyConcept: Ventral spinocerebellar tract

questions.subject: physiology
questions.question: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries which sensations?
questions.explanation: The lateral spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature sensation after crossing in the spinal cord, while fine touch and vibration are carried by the dorsal columns.
questions.keyConcept: Lateral spinothalamic tract: pain and temperature.
